explainer_content.short_definition: The early lane where R&B and gospel-rooted singing become broad pop through hooks, strings, dance rhythm, and unmistakable lead voices.
explainer_content.history_capsule: Early soul-pop crossover sits between first-wave rock and the later soul/funk universe. Ray Charles, Sam Cooke, Jackie Wilson, Ben E. King, Etta James, The Isley Brothers, early Motown, and related records show how Black R&B and gospel language entered mass pop without losing emotional pressure.
explainer_content.why_it_mattered: It helped create the blueprint for soul as pop language: lead-vocal testimony, rhythm-section lift, hook clarity, and arrangements polished enough for wide radio play.
explainer_content.what_made_it_distinct: Compared with doo-wop or teen-idol pop, the lead voice carries more church-derived urgency, the groove is heavier, and the arrangement often balances raw feeling with pop elegance.
what_to_listen_for: Gospel melisma moved into secular lyrics
A bass or piano figure that hooks the record
Strings or backing vocals smoothing an R&B core
Dance rhythm under adult emotional weight
